title: Computational Kesten–Stigum threshold
formal:
Do there exist a fixed integer \(q\ge5\), fixed rational numbers \(a>b>0\), a fixed real \(\delta>0\), and one uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) such that
\[(a-b)^2<q\bigl(a+(q-1)b\bigr)\]
and, for every sufficiently large integer \(n\), the symmetric stochastic block model defined below satisfies
\[\mathbb E\bigl[\operatorname{ov}(A(G),\sigma)\bigr]\ge\frac1q+\delta?\]
All model parameters and the algorithm are chosen once, independently of \(n\). The expectation is over the planted labels, the graph and the algorithm's random bits.
definitions:
For \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), draw the hidden labels \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n\) independently and uniformly from \([q]\). Conditional on these labels, independently include each unordered pair \(\{i,j\}\), \(i\ne j\), as an edge with probability \(a/n\) when \(\sigma_i=\sigma_j\), and with probability \(b/n\) otherwise. The graph is simple and undirected. Take integer \(n\ge\max\{1,\lceil a\rceil\}\), so these probabilities are valid. Groups have equal prior probabilities; their sizes are not conditioned to be exactly equal.

The input to \(A\) is this single graph on the named vertices \([n]\), encoded by its explicit binary adjacency matrix together with \(n\). The constants \(q,a,b\) are known to the algorithm and may be incorporated into its finite description. No hidden labels, correlated side information or auxiliary sample graphs are supplied. On every graph input and every random tape, the algorithm halts within \(K(n+1)^k\) ordinary Turing-machine bit steps for some fixed constants \(K,k\), and outputs a vector \(\widehat\sigma\in[q]^n\). Randomness consists of independent unbiased bits. Uniform means one finite program for all input lengths, with no length-dependent advice. The program, runtime constants and recovery advantage may depend on the chosen \(q,a,b\), but not on \(n\).

For label vectors \(u,v\in[q]^n\), set
\[\operatorname{ov}(u,v)=\max_{\pi\in S_q}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{u_i=\pi(v_i)\},\]
where \(S_q\) is the finite set of all permutations of \([q]\) and the indicator is one exactly when its condition holds. Relabelling communities does not change their quality. Output labels may be unused. The maximum is part of the mathematical performance measure; the algorithm does not know \(\sigma\) and is not asked to compute this maximum. The chance baseline \(1/q\) is the limiting baseline for fixed \(q\), not a claim that the finite-sample expectation of a maximized random overlap equals exactly \(1/q\).

Write
\[d=\frac{a+(q-1)b}{q},\qquad \theta=\frac{a-b}{a+(q-1)b}.\]
Here \(d\) is the limiting expected degree; the finite graph has expected degree \((1-1/n)d\). The Kesten–Stigum threshold is \(d\theta^2=1\), and the required strict inequality is \(d\theta^2<1\). The case \(a>b\) is assortative: edges are more likely within a group. The card asks for a fixed positive expected recovery advantage for all \(n\ge n_0\), for one finite \(n_0\); it does not replace that requirement by a probability tending to one, a statement only on a subsequence, or a community count growing with \(n\). There is no separate promise of information-theoretic recoverability: a successful algorithmic example would itself prove it.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the exact existential proposition. A positive answer must give one fixed eligible \(q,a,b,\delta,A\), a uniform worst-case polynomial runtime bound, and a finite \(n_0\) for which the expected-overlap inequality holds for every eligible \(n\ge n_0\). A negative answer must exclude every such choice: for every eligible fixed parameter triple, uniform polynomial-time randomized algorithm and positive \(\delta\), and every proposed \(n_0\), some eligible \(n\ge n_0\) must violate that expected-overlap inequality. Information-theoretic recovery with unlimited computation, conditional computational hardness, lower bounds for a restricted estimator class, and results with growing \(q\) do not settle the proposition. This is exact yes/no acceptance, with no numerical tolerance applied to the threshold or the quantifiers.
why: Determine whether the canonical local signal threshold is a true barrier for every efficient algorithm in a basic model of network inference.

importance.reason: A central, sharply parameterized computational-versus-statistical gap linking sparse random graphs, inference, message passing and average-case complexity.

progress.text: Abbe and Sandon establish efficient recovery strictly above the threshold for fixed community counts; the checked preprint supplies the symmetric-model overlap comparison.

Banks, Moore, Neeman and Netrapalli prove below-threshold information-theoretic recovery in suitable assortative regimes with at least eleven communities. This recovery need not run in polynomial time.
The revised conditional lower-bound paper relates restricted low-degree testing conjectures to matrix recovery hardness, retaining explicit model and parameter assumptions.

The revised many-community paper gives below-threshold polynomial algorithms when the number of groups grows sufficiently quickly, and separate bounds on low-degree estimators. Neither is an unconditional settlement for all algorithms at fixed q,a,b.

status_note: Source-open. On 16 September 2026 the four primary papers were checked at the definition and main-theorem passages identified in their references, including the 23 August 2026 revision. Above-threshold algorithms, below-threshold information-theoretic recovery, restricted conditional hardness and growing-community algorithms leave the stated fixed-parameter unconditional question open in these sources. Bounded current-work searches found no matching settlement. Full cited proofs have not been independently verified or formalized in Lean.

context_blocks.text: Community detection asks whether the edges of a network reveal an underlying partition. Here every vertex has the same expected degree, regardless of its group. Consequently, sorting vertices by degree cannot directly identify their communities. The signal is in the pattern of connections between vertices, and each vertex has only a constant expected number of observations even as the network grows.

The target is deliberately much weaker than recovering every label. A constant-degree graph has many isolated vertices, whose memberships cannot be inferred from their incident edges. Weak recovery asks only for a fixed improvement over random guessing on average. Permuting all community names must be allowed: renaming the hidden groups changes neither the graph distribution nor the quality of an inferred partition.

The quantity \(d\theta ^{2}\) compares the growth in the number of observed neighbours with the decay of label information along an edge. In a local tree approximation, d describes branching and \(\theta\) describes how much a child’s label remembers its parent’s label. This explains why the value one is a natural boundary for algorithms based on propagation of small correlations. It does not by itself prove an impossibility result for algorithms that use the whole graph.

Abbe and Sandon prove efficient recovery above this boundary for every fixed number of communities. Their method uses an acyclic form of belief propagation and addresses the effect of cycles in the finite graph. This supplies the algorithmic side of the proposed threshold. The question asks whether a qualitatively different method can succeed strictly below it in the assortative case \(a>b\).

There really are parameters for which the graph contains useful information below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. Banks, Moore, Neeman and Netrapalli establish such regimes for at least eleven groups in the assortative model. Their recovery argument permits exponential computation, searching over sufficiently plausible partitions. Their five-group statement concerns the disassortative case, where between-group edges are more likely; that is a different parameter range from this card.

This produces a concrete computational-versus-statistical puzzle. The missing labels are not intrinsically unidentifiable everywhere below the boundary, yet known efficient methods do not recover them throughout the information-theoretically possible region. An affirmative answer to this card would refute the universal fixed-community barrier with a single parameter example. A negative answer would establish that the obstruction is computational wherever recovery is statistically possible.

Ding, Hua, Slot and Steurer derive recovery hardness from a restricted, unproved low-degree conjecture about testing. Their recovery statistic correlates an estimated matrix with the centred matrix of community co-membership. Theorem A.1 uses integer average-degree parameters and a signal parameter in [0,1], so it should not be quoted as an unconditional theorem for every rational pair a,b allowed here. Under its hypotheses it supplies strong evidence for a computational barrier, not a proof excluding every polynomial-time algorithm.

The precise conjecture in that paper also matters. Its bounded test functions must have expectation bounded below under the planted distribution. The authors explain that a broader earlier version was refuted using rare events. Thus citing a generic “low-degree conjecture” without stating that a hypothesis remains unproved would erase both the conditional nature of the result and an actual correction in the underlying evidence.

The August 2026 revision of Chin, Mossel, Sohn and Wein proves efficient recovery in some regimes below the usual threshold when the number of communities grows as n^χ with χ greater than one half by a fixed margin. In that scaling, within-community edge intensity also grows. Here q,a,b are fixed before n tends to infinity. The new algorithm therefore does not provide the example requested by this card. Their accompanying lower bounds apply to low-degree polynomial estimators, not to all algorithms.

Settling this problem would test whether a threshold suggested by local propagation describes all efficient global algorithms in a basic random graph model. A new algorithm would identify exploitable structure missed by the familiar threshold calculation. A rigorous barrier would give a particularly clean example in which unlimited inference and efficient inference have different capabilities, with the data distribution specified by only three constants.

sentences: A sparse stochastic block model hides a fixed number of equally likely community labels in a random graph.
The question asks whether any fixed assortative parameters below the Kesten–Stigum threshold allow polynomial-time recovery with a constant expected advantage over chance.
The algorithm receives one graph, and success is measured after the best permutation of the community names.
Information can survive below the threshold, but known computational barriers retain conjectural or restricted-estimator assumptions.
Recent algorithms with a growing number of communities do not supply the fixed-parameter example required here.
